explanations.answer: Those who work hard among them
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The writers ask the brothers to "…acknowledge those who work diligently among you, who care for you in the Lord and who admonish you." (1 Thessalonians 5:12) That's three jobs in one sentence: working hard, caring and admonishing. The letter says to notice the people doing them.

Nope, no city officials in this verse, friend. The writers point to people right among the brothers, those who "…work diligently among you…" (1 Thessalonians 5:12) These are folks who care for the brothers in the Lord and admonish them. The next verse says to hold them in highest regard because of their work. (1 Thessalonians 5:13)

Not quite, friend. The writers aren't pointing far away at all. They point to those "among you," the ones who work diligently, care for the brothers in the Lord and admonish them. (1 Thessalonians 5:12) Jerusalem doesn't come up in this passage, so the hard workers are right there with the brothers.

That's it, friend. The verse says to "…admonish the unruly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone." (1 Thessalonians 5:14) Four kinds of care, and each one fits a different need. A nervous heart gets a hand on the shoulder, not a lecture.

Close, but that word isn't in the verse, friend. The fainthearted are told to be encouraged, and the admonishing is for the unruly. (1 Thessalonians 5:14) Rebuking a scared person is like using the rolling pin to fix a squeaky hinge. Wrong tool, and now everybody's nervous.

Not this one, friend. The letter never says to avoid anybody here. It says to "…encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone." (1 Thessalonians 5:14) The fainthearted get closer attention, not less.

Not what the text says, friend. The verse ends with "…be patient with everyone." (1 Thessalonians 5:14) Everyone. No fine print and no outsider exception. I'd read it twice, because that's a tall order and it's right there in black and white.

Right, friend. The letter says "…be patient with everyone." and everyone means everyone. (1 Thessalonians 5:14) There's no insider-only section in that sentence. Just a short, big command, and I'm still working on it myself.

explanations.answer: That no one repays evil for evil
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The letter says, "Make sure that no one repays evil for evil." (1 Thessalonians 5:15) Notice it says no one, so it's a job for the whole group. Put the phone down, friend, and leave that reply unsent.

explanations.answer: That the leaders settle it quickly
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but the letter doesn't say that here. It says, "Make sure that no one repays evil for evil." (1 Thessalonians 5:15) The command is aimed at the brothers themselves, and it says nothing about handing the problem off. So that's on all of us, and I'd better keep my mustache off the keyboard.

The verse doesn't wait on an apology, friend. It says, "Make sure that no one repays evil for evil." (1 Thessalonians 5:15) Nothing there about who has to say sorry first. The command lands on the one who was wronged, and that's the part that stings.

explanations.answer: Always rejoice and never stop praying
explanations.explanation: That's the pair, friend. "Rejoice at all times. Pray without ceasing." (1 Thessalonians 5:16-17) At all times and without ceasing. No days off from either one. I'll be honest, I can barely go a whole afternoon without checking the timer, and the letter says never stop.

explanations.answer: Rejoice on good days and pray every morning
explanations.explanation: Close in spirit, but the letter asks for more. It says, "Rejoice at all times. Pray without ceasing." (1 Thessalonians 5:16-17) Not just the good days and not just the mornings. The words are "…at all times." and "without ceasing," and those leave no gaps.

explanations.answer: Rejoice in private and pray in public
explanations.explanation: Not in this verse, friend. The letter says, "Rejoice at all times. Pray without ceasing." (1 Thessalonians 5:16-17) It says nothing about where to do either one. The weight is on when: at all times, without ceasing.

Yes, friend. The letter says, "Give thanks in every circumstance, for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus." (1 Thessalonians 5:18) Every circumstance, and the letter says this is God's will for them in Christ Jesus. That's a big one, so give thanks even when the batch comes out flat.

This one is true, friend, and I know it sounds like too much. The verse says, "Give thanks in every circumstance, for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus." (1 Thessalonians 5:18) Every circumstance, no exceptions listed, and it's tied to God's will for them in Christ Jesus. I'd check the verse twice too, but it says what it says.

That's it, friend. "Do not treat prophecies with contempt, but test all things. Hold fast to what is good." (1 Thessalonians 5:20-21) No sneering at prophecies, and no swallowing everything whole either. You test, and then you hold on to the good.

Not quite, friend. The letter says, "…but test all things." (1 Thessalonians 5:21) Testing and accepting everything are two different things. You don't taste-test every cookie and then claim they were all perfect.

The letter doesn't say that, friend. After telling them not to treat prophecies with contempt, it says, "…but test all things." (1 Thessalonians 5:20-21) The instruction goes to the brothers themselves. They're the ones who do the testing and then hold fast to what is good.

Right, friend. The letter says, "Abstain from every form of evil." (1 Thessalonians 5:22) Just before it comes "…test all things. Hold fast to what is good." (1 Thessalonians 5:21) So good gets the grip, and evil gets the cold shoulder. Every form means every form, not just the big ones.

Not this one, friend. Prophecies come up a verse earlier, where the brothers are told not to treat them with contempt. (1 Thessalonians 5:20) Then the letter says, "Abstain from every form of evil." (1 Thessalonians 5:22) Prophecy gets tested, and evil gets left alone.

Fasting isn't anywhere in this passage, friend. The verse says, "Abstain from every form of evil." (1 Thessalonians 5:22) That's the match for holding fast to what is good. Good gets the grip, and evil gets the cold shoulder.

Careful, friend. The letter asks for more than that. It says, "…may your entire spirit, soul, and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ." (1 Thessalonians 5:23) Spirit, soul and body, the whole person. A part-time blameless job isn't on the menu.

Right, friend. It isn't only the soul. The letter says, "…may your entire spirit, soul, and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ." (1 Thessalonians 5:23) The whole person is covered, and that's good news for every one of us.

Yes, friend. The letter says, "The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it." (1 Thessalonians 5:24) The "it" is the sanctifying and keeping blameless from the verse before. The letter puts that big job on the One who calls. That's a relief, because I couldn't carry that batch myself.

Good thought, but the letter points somewhere else. It says, "The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it." (1 Thessalonians 5:24) The leaders were just mentioned a few verses back, but this promise rests on the One who calls. Faithful is His word here.

Not this time, friend. The writers aren't promising it themselves. They say, "The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it." (1 Thessalonians 5:24) Look at who gets the credit: the One who calls. The writers just pass the word along.

Yes, friend. The writer says, "I charge you before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers." (1 Thessalonians 5:27) Charged before the Lord, so it's no small request. The letter is meant to be read to all the brothers.

This one is true, friend. The writer says, "I charge you before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers." (1 Thessalonians 5:27) Charged before the Lord, and the reading is for all the brothers. The card says exactly that.
